areas_of_law: Unjust/unfair dismissal or discipline of dependent contractor/employee
issues: Whether the reverse onus/statutory presumption under s. 98(4) of the Canada Labour Code applies, shifting the burden to the employer to prove the decision to stop dispatching the driver was in no way related to his union/representative activity

What the employer must establish to discharge that burden - i.e., that the decision was based on a legitimate, non-discriminatory business reason wholly unconnected to anti-union animus, on a balance of probabilities
Whether the timing of the decision (during the pendency of the certification application, shortly after objections were withdrawn) supports an inference of anti-union animus

Whether the employer's failure to call the dispatcher or any witness with first-hand knowledge, and reliance on unnamed informants, old warning letters and hearsay, is sufficient to meet its burden or instead undermines its case
Whether the worker is properly characterized as a dependent contractor/employee for the purposes of Canada Labour Code protections, given he is an 'owner-operator'
Whether the employer's stated reason (working elsewhere while on medical leave, missed Mondays) constitutes a credible, sufficient, non-pretextual justification
What weight/adverse inference should be drawn from a party's failure to call an available witness with material first-hand knowledge (dispatcher)
Whether the employer's assertion of ignorance of the union/certification is credible or rebuttable given the known certification proceedings and counsel's involvement
key_facts: Client is an owner-operator hauling marine containers for a federally regulated trucking company
He was elected drivers' representative during a port dispute and remained active in the union seeking to certify the employer's drivers
Certification application filed roughly a year before the cut-off; employer opposed via counsel; objections dropped shortly before client was cut off
Client was off work with a non-work-related sprained ankle, provided a medical note, and called dispatch regularly once able to wear a safety boot, being told work was slow
He was then told he would no longer be dispatched because someone allegedly saw him working elsewhere
At the hearing, only the employer's owner testified, claiming no knowledge of the union or the client's involvement
Employer relied on unnamed informants, old warning letters, and a list of missed Mondays
Employer did not call the dispatcher or anyone with first-hand knowledge of the events
All complained-of conduct occurred while the certification application was pending
causes_of_action: Unfair labour practice complaint under s. 94(3) Canada Labour Code (interference with/discrimination against employee for union activity)
Reverse-onus statutory presumption under s. 98(4) CLC that anti-union animus was a reason for the decision once complainant shows union activity and adverse treatment during pendency of certification
Possible unjust dismissal complaint under s. 240 CLC if worker found to be a dependent contractor/employee, not a true independent contractor
candidate_statutes: Canada Labour Code, Part I (Industrial Relations) - ss. 94-98 (unfair labour practices), s. 97 (reverse onus complaint), s. 98(4) presumption
Canada Labour Code, Part III - s. 240 (unjust dismissal, if worker qualifies as employee/dependent contractor)
